471.event_title: Japan secures the Anglo-Japanese Alliance before facing Russia
471.place: London, United Kingdom, and Tokyo, Japan
471.event: In 1902 Japan concluded an alliance with Britain under which each partner would stay neutral if the other went to war with one power, but would come to its aid if a second power joined in against it. With this safeguard against a coalition, the Japanese government took a firmer line against Russian advances in Manchuria and Korea, and in 1904 it went to war with Russia.
471.explanation: Japan measured not only its own forces against Russia's but also the allies each side could call upon, and arranged matters so that it would face Russia alone.
471.tie_back: The kural tells a ruler to weigh the task, his own strength, the enemy's strength and the strength of the allies on each side, and the alliance was Japan's way of fixing that last term in its favour before acting.
471._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of weighing allies before acting, though the sources do not set out Japan's full four-part calculation in detail.

472.event_title: Thor Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki raft crosses the Pacific
472.place: Callao, Peru, to Raroia, Tuamotu Islands (French Polynesia)
472.event: To test his theory that South Americans could have reached Polynesia, the Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl and five companions built a raft of balsa logs modelled on early South American designs and set out from Callao, Peru. Critics had predicted the raft would break up within weeks, but after about 101 days and some 4,300 miles it reached the reef of Raroia in the Tuamotu Islands.
472.explanation: The voyage showed that such a crossing was physically possible, though scholars did not accept Heyerdahl's wider theory of Polynesian origins.
472.tie_back: The kural says nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do, learn what the task needs and keep steadily at it, and the Kon-Tiki crew prepared carefully and held to their course for over three months.
472._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of preparation and steady persistence achieving a feat others thought impossible, though the sources say little about Heyerdahl's self-assessment.

473.event_title: The Burke and Wills expedition breaks down on the way back
473.place: Victoria to the Gulf of Carpentaria, Australia
473.event: The Victorian Exploring Expedition under Robert O'Hara Burke set out to cross Australia from south to north. Burke split his party, pushed ahead from Cooper Creek with a small group and inadequate provisions, and came near the Gulf of Carpentaria in February 1861, but on the return journey the men weakened, missed the depot party at Cooper Creek by hours, and Burke and William Wills died at the end of June 1861. A royal commission later censured Burke for dividing his party and setting out with inadequate supplies.
473.explanation: The expedition reached its goal but collapsed on the way back, because its leader had not matched the pace of his plans to the strength of his men and supplies.
473.tie_back: The kural says many who did not know the measure of their strength have broken down midway, and Burke's party gave out on the homeward stretch of its journey.
473._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of an enterprise breaking down midway through misjudged resources, though the sources frame the fault as poor decisions rather than enthusiasm.

474.event_title: Charles XII of Sweden is defeated at Poltava
474.event: After years of victories in the Great Northern War, Charles XII of Sweden invaded Russia and turned south into Ukraine, far from his supplies. Though wounded in the foot, he chose to attack Peter the Great's fortified camp at Poltava, the assault failed, and three days later most of the Swedish army surrendered at Perevolochna. Charles escaped to Ottoman territory, where he spent about five years trying in vain to persuade the Ottomans to attack Russia.
474.explanation: A king who had won many battles staked his army on one more deep campaign and lost Sweden's standing as a great power.
474.tie_back: The kural warns that one who misjudges his own measure and acts without regard to others is quickly ruined, and Poltava destroyed Charles's army in a single day.
474._accuracy_note: Fits the ruin that follows misjudged strength, but the kural's charge of self-admiration is an inner state that the sources do not document.

475.event_title: The cities of the Lombard League defeat Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano
475.event: Northern Italian cities, among them Milan, Venice, Mantua, Padua and Brescia, formed the Lombard League in 1167 to resist the Holy Roman emperor Frederick I Barbarossa's attempts to curb their self-government. At Legnano in 1176 the League's army, led by Milan, routed the imperial forces. Frederick agreed to a truce and in the Peace of Constance of 1183 granted the cities self-government in return for their allegiance.
475.explanation: No single city could have defeated the emperor, but together they broke his power in northern Italy.
475.tie_back: The kural's cart of peacock feathers shows how many light loads together break a strong axle, and the old commentators read it as a warning that small foes combined can overwhelm a great ruler, as the Lombard cities did.
475._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of Parimelazhagar's reading of the kural; the literal image of a load piled beyond measure is less directly matched.

476.event_title: The Ottoman siege of Vienna fails
476.event: The Ottoman grand vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha led a vast army to besiege Vienna in July 1683. On 12 September a relief army under King John III Sobieski of Poland attacked at the Kahlenberg and routed the besiegers. Kara Mustafa was put to death in Belgrade on the sultan's orders on 25 December 1683, and in the wars that followed the Ottomans lost large territories in central Europe.
476.explanation: The siege marked the furthest point of a long Ottoman advance, and the attempt to push beyond it began a long retreat.
476.tie_back: The kural says that those who climb beyond the tip of the branch fall to their death, and Kara Mustafa's push to Vienna went past the limit his empire could support and cost him his life.
476._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of overreach at the height of power ending in personal ruin and lasting decline.

477.event: The merchant and banker Jakob Fugger endowed a walled settlement of homes for needy Catholic citizens of Augsburg, setting the annual rent at one Rhenish guilder and providing in the foundation deed that it should last forever. Funded by the Fugger foundations' endowment, the Fuggerei still houses about 150 people, and its annual base rent remains the equivalent of one guilder, about 88 euro cents.
477.explanation: Because the gift was set up within the means of a lasting endowment, it has kept giving for five centuries without being used up.
477.tie_back: The kural says giving in the right way and within one's measure is how wealth is preserved even while it is given, and the Fuggerei is a gift that has outlived its giver by 500 years.
477._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of measured, sustainable generosity; the sources describe the endowment's durability rather than Fugger's own reasoning.

478.event_title: Andrew Jackson's government pays off the national debt
478.event: Andrew Jackson came to office determined to end the national debt, and his administration used revenue from the sale of federal lands while he vetoed many spending bills. By January 1835 all of the government's interest-bearing debt had been paid off, the only time in United States history, and that year the government ran a large surplus that Congress distributed to the states. Within a short time, an economic downturn led the government to borrow again.
478.explanation: For a brief period the United States government spent less than it took in, until it had no debt at all.
478.tie_back: The kural says that a narrow income does no harm so long as outgoings are not wider, and Jackson's government cleared its debts by keeping spending below its revenue.
478._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of spending kept below income, but the debt-free state did not last, and the policy is linked by historians to the Panic of 1837.

479.event_title: Rembrandt loses his house and collection
479.event: In 1639 Rembrandt bought a large house on the Jodenbreestraat in Amsterdam, and he spent heavily on paintings, prints, antiquities and studio props. Mounting debts left him unable to keep up the payments, and in 1656 an official inventory was made of his possessions, nearly all of which were then sold at auction. The house was sold in 1658, and Rembrandt moved to a rented home on the Rozengracht, where he died in 1669.
479.explanation: The most celebrated painter of his city lived in apparent prosperity for years before his household and collection were dispersed.
479.tie_back: The kural says the life of one who does not live within his means seems to flourish and then vanishes, as Rembrandt's grand house and collection did.
479._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of outward prosperity collapsing for want of living within one's means, though Rembrandt's art and reputation, unlike his wealth, did not vanish.

480.event: Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with a very large caravan carrying great quantities of gold. When he stopped in Cairo, he spent and gave away gold so lavishly that its value there fell, and the market had still not recovered some twelve years later.
480.explanation: Generosity on such a scale became famous across the Mediterranean world but also showed that even vast wealth can be poured out faster than is wise.
480.tie_back: The kural warns that giving without weighing the limits of one's resources quickly exhausts them, and Mansa Musa's journey is the best-known case of giving on a scale beyond measure.
480._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: the sources document lavish, unmeasured giving, but not that it ruined Mali's own wealth.
